transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Tom Greene (Tannery CTO), Maya Ortiz (Lead Backend), Evan Li (Security)

Summary:
- Intro and goals: figure out how Tannery will integrate Redwood (hosted vs dedicated vs private), focus on gateway/proxy, SDK compatibility (LangChain/LlamaIndex), rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks for their platform.
- Security discussion: SSO/SAML, SOC2, KMS and audit logs, private VPC/on-prem considerations.
- Technical asks: sample traffic for benchmarking, SDK examples, latency vs cost tradeoffs, caching and KV cache behaviour.
- Agreed next steps and owners as action items.

Topics:
- Integration patterns: sidecar vs gateway vs proxy
- LangChain & LlamaIndex adapter compatibility
- Rate limiting, tenant quotas, burst capacity
- Observability hooks: traces, token-level cost breakdown, sampling

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Okay, hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Priya, our systems SE. Do you want to kick off with quick intros, Tom?
[00:07] Tom (Tannery CTO): Yeah, thanks Alex. I'm Tom, CTO at Tannery Labs. We build internal knowledge agents for e-comm ops, heavy traffic during promos. Maya runs backend and infra, Evan is on security.
[00:14] Maya (Tannery): Hey all.
[00:15] Evan (Tannery): Hi.
[00:16] Priya (Redwood SE): Hi, good to meet you. Quick agenda — we'll cover integration patterns, SDK compatibility, quota/rate models, and then security/compliance. Sound good?
[00:24] Tom: Perfect. Our main question — do we go hosted to move fast, or dedicate capacity, or run private in our VPC? We also have an existing gateway/proxy layer, so we want to see how Redwood fits in.
[00:35] Alex: Great. Maybe high-level first — hosted for fast onboarding, dedicated reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput, and private for VPC or on-prem when you need isolation. But the integration pattern really depends on how you want routing and auth to behave.
[00:46] Tom: Right, and we have a custom gateway today — basically a proxy that handles tenant auth, rate limits, and does prompt templating. We use LangChain in some services and LlamaIndex in others, and we want to avoid rewriting everything.
[00:58] Priya: Good to know. Redwood's SDKs have first-class adapters for LangChain and a community LlamaIndex connector. We can share code snippets, but we also support a proxy approach — you can keep your gateway and call Redwood behind it.
[01:12] Maya: If we keep our proxy, what about rate limits? We have per-tenant quotas and burst allowances. Will we double-count or have conflicts?
[01:20] Priya: You can keep tenant-level enforcement in your gateway and use Redwood's per-key quotas as a second layer. Many customers use the gateway for policy and Redwood for global rate control and SLO-based throttling. The important part is passing consistent headers — e.g., x-tenant-id, x-request-priority — so Redwood routing can map to dedicated pools or hosted fallback.
[01:35] Evan: Quick security question — if we go private (VPC), how does KMS work? We need HSM-backed keys for encryption at rest.
[01:42] Alex: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS integrations, including HSM providers. We'll include the architecture doc in the pack. For Hosted and Dedicated, we offer envelope encryption with customer keys where possible.
[01:54] Evan: Great. Please send SOC2 evidence too.
[01:57] Alex: Yep, we'll include SOC2 and our security Q&A in the next email.
[02:02] Tom: Back to integration — we do both synchronous chat and async batch embeddings. How does Redwood handle batching and KV cache when using a gateway?
[02:10] Priya: Two things — runtime supports continuous batching and prefix/KV caching. If your gateway forwards streaming chat requests directly, the runtime can still batch on the backend as long as you use compatible streaming semantics. For embeddings/batch jobs, we recommend using Redwood SDK batch endpoints to get better packing. There's an edge case with very small requests where a gateway adds 10–20ms but batching saves tokens overall.
[02:32] Maya: And the KV cache — we sometimes have prompt prefixes repeated across requests; can Redwood share cache across model instances?
[02:39] Priya: Yes, KV cache is per-serving shard but we have shared prefix caches for common templates. There's some leaky specifics — it's not a global LRU across all nodes in every config. I'll share a short note about K-V cash — sorry, K-V cache — ha, speech-to-text does that — on how it behaves in dedicated vs hosted.
[02:57] Tom: Haha. That's fine.
[03:00] [Speaker 1]: Can I ask about SDK languages? We have services in Go, Python, and a lightweight Node edge.
[03:05] Alex: We have official SDKs for Python and Node, Go is community but maintained; we also publish HTTP API examples. The best practice for LangChain is to use the Redwood Python SDK or direct HTTP with the LangChain adapter. For LlamaIndex we can share a connector — it's been patchy due to versions but we've got recent compatibility notes.
[03:22] Maya: For the PoC we want minimal changes — ideally we wrap calls in our gateway and swap endpoints. How much code change is that?
[03:29] Priya: Minimal — if you keep your proxy and just point a route to Redwood, you'd do header mapping and key rotation. For LangChain clients you may only need to change the model_name/url and a token param. We'll provide a gateway example showing header mappings and fallback policies.
[03:44] Tom: Fallback policies — can Redwood route to cheaper model variants or regions automatically when capacity is constrained?
[03:51] Priya: Yes, smart routing can fallback to model variants (e.g., a quantized variant) or different capacity tiers. You can configure policy rules: latency SLO first, cost threshold, or region. We also support canary rollouts per-model version.
[04:05] Tom: Cool. For observability, we need distributed traces and token-level cost breakdowns in our dashboards. What do you expose?
[04:13] Alex: Redwood Console exports traces (Jaeger compatible), per-request token accounting, per-model latency heatmaps, and you can push logs to your SIEM via syslog or an S3 sink. There are tracing hooks you can instrument in your gateway so you get end-to-end traces.
[04:29] Evan: Do you expose the raw prompts in logs? We need to keep PII out.
[04:33] Priya: By default we redact sensitive payloads in logs and you can set retention and redaction policies. For compliance-heavy customers we disable prompt retention and only store token counts and hashes. We'll include the redaction config options.
[04:46] Maya: About quotas again — we have tenants with spiky usage, need burst credit. Can Redwood honor burst above committed?
[04:53] Alex: Yes, Dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscaling. Hosted customers can request burst allowances based on plan and also use fallback to lower-cost models to handle spikes. For strict budget controls you can apply token caps per-key in the gateway and enforce them upstream.
[05:07] Tom: Any hard limits on concurrent KV cache sizes or sequence lengths? We push up to 8k tokens for some flows, occasionally 32k for doc recaps.
[05:16] Priya: Runtime supports up to 32k in hosted for certain models; larger sequences may require dedicated configs. There are memory tradeoffs — longer contexts increase per-request memory and affect batching. We'll share our performance matrix with sequence-length vs throughput.
[05:31] Maya: We saw mention in docs about continuous batching and tokens per second metrics — can we run a small benchmark that mimics our pattern (many short chat messages)?
[05:39] Alex: Absolutely. We ask you to provide sample traffic and typical prompt shapes — number of tokens, frequency, and distribution. We'll run latency and cost estimates and return a bench report.
[05:49] Tom: Regarding auth — we want SSO for console access and service-to-service keys for the gateway. How granular is RBAC?
[05:56] Priya: RBAC maps to teams and routes — you can create API keys scoped to routes, models, and quotas. SSO is SAML/OIDC with SCIM for user sync. For private deployments SCIM hooks can point to your IdP.
[06:09] Evan: Do you support audit logs with immutable storage for audits?
[06:13] Alex: Yes, audit logs can be exported to a customer S3 bucket with object immutability and we also provide an append-only audit stream for Dedicated/Private.
[06:22] Maya: Any gotchas when using LangChain retries with Redwood streaming? We've seen duplicate tokens when the client retries.
[06:30] Priya: Good point — clients should implement idempotency keys for retries. Our runtime supports idempotency tokens which prevent duplicate consumption when the same request is retried within a window. We'll show examples for LangChain retry hooks.
[06:44] Tom: Are there prebuilt connectors for our gateway (it's based on Envoy)?
[06:49] Priya: We have Envoy examples — route filters that inject headers and pass tokens. We'll give you an envoy filter snippet and a simple sidecar example if you prefer that pattern.
[06:58] Evan: From a compliance standpoint, if we go Hosted, can you guarantee data residency EU only?
[07:04] Alex: Hosted can be regionally pinned in supported regions. For strict residency and contractual obligations, Private in your VPC or on-prem is recommended. We'll note the residency options in the security pack.
[07:16] Maya: On billing and meter — do you return per-request token metadata so we can reconcile costs?
[07:21] Alex: Yes, both per-request token counts and per-model costs are available via the API and Console. You can ingest via our usage CSVs or call a usage API.
[07:29] [00:07:30 approx - brief cross-talk about calendar times]
[07:35] Tom: For the PoC scope, we'd like to prove: 1) latency for short chat flows, 2) embedding pipeline throughput, 3) fallback policy during spike. Is that reasonable?
[07:44] Priya: Totally. Typical PoC: 2 weeks, initial sandbox credentials, bench runs, and then config tuning. We'll propose a pilot plan in the PRD.
[07:53] Maya: Any advice on reducing token costs without hurting quality?
[07:57] Priya: Use template compression, prefix caching, and offload deterministic transforms to your gateway. Also quantized model variants for non-core flows and response length caps. Redwood Optimize can analyze token waste and suggest quantization profiles.
[08:10] Evan: Any mention of competitors or migration risk? We heard about OpenAI and Anthropic — do migrations maintain parity?
[08:18] Alex: There's always some difference. We provide inference profiles and benchmark results for comparable open models. Part of the PoC is to validate quality on your prompt set.
[08:27] Tom: Let's recap next steps.
[08:29] Alex: Recap: Alex will send the security pack and SOC2 docs plus KMS notes by 3/10. Priya will post SDK samples, LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters, and an Envoy filter example by 3/11. Tannery will supply sample traffic and compliance controls list by 3/12. We schedule PoC kickoff week of 3/15.
[08:46] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks, everyone.
[08:48] Maya: Thanks.
[08:49] Evan: Thanks.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings ("K-V cash" for KV cache), timestamps approximate (every 30–90s), speaker attributions mostly accurate but auto-transcribe sometimes labels generics.
